strengths: Clear, well-motivated extension of mechanistic interpretability methodologies from LLMs (e.g., Ortu et al., 2024) to vision-language models, addressing the timely and critical problem of multimodal knowledge conflicts.

Convincing functional localization findings: the paper reveals a clear division of labor where upper-layer MLP blocks reinforce parametric/factual knowledge, whereas specific late-layer attention heads promote visually grounded counterfactual tokens.

Rigorous experimental validation featuring both causal intervention (multiplicative reweighting of attention heads) and ablation studies (visual patch ablation), supported by necessary negative controls (e.g., intervening on random heads and ablating random patches).
Practical demonstration that attention attribution from identified counterfactual heads pinpoints visually anomalous regions more precisely than standard gradient-based attribution methods.
Well-structured presentation, clear visualizations (e.g., Figures 2–5), and thorough documentation of prompts and generation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The dataset size is relatively modest (originating from 500 WHOOPS! images and filtered down to ~430 test instances per model), which leaves open questions about generalization across a broader variety of domains and subtle knowledge conflict types.

The evaluation is restricted to next-token prediction (isolated to single-token completions). While this design choice ensures tractability for logit lens and mechanistic probing, it leaves open whether these localized mechanisms operate identically during multi-token free-form text generation.

The intervention mechanism (Equations 4 and 5) applies direct multiplicative scaling to attention matrices at test time rather than activation patching or learned steering vectors; while effective, the scaling parameter is heuristic and requires careful clipping to prevent degenerative text generation.

strengths: Clear and well-formulated mechanistic study tackling an important and timely problem: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between visual inputs and parametric commonsense knowledge.

Consistent and insightful findings across two distinct architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b), showing a division of labor where upper-layer MLPs promote internal factual knowledge while specific late-layer attention heads promote visually grounded counterfactual predictions.
Convincing causal verification via targeted attention interventions and ablation experiments, accompanied by random-head and random-patch control baselines.
Practical demonstration that attention from identified counterfactual heads serves as an effective attribution map, localizing semantic anomaly regions more accurately than gradient-based baselines.
weaknesses: The analysis is constrained to single next-token completions at the final prompt position, which simplifies the multi-token autoregressive generation dynamic where knowledge conflicts may unfold differently over time.
The dataset size is relatively small (around 430 filtered examples derived from the 500 images of the WHOOPS! dataset), limiting the diversity of syntactic templates and domain coverage.

The interventions on attention weights, while theoretically illuminating, can noticeably degrade general fluency and distribution shift (as shown by the KL divergence and generation quality drop around |lambda| >= 3), meaning the mechanistic insights do not yet translate into a practical inference-time mitigation method.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: understanding the internal mechanistic processes governing multimodal knowledge conflicts between parametric knowledge and conflicting visual input in VLMs.
Methodologically sound and thorough: combines Logit Lens inspection with bidirectional causal attention interventions and patch-level ablation experiments.

Rigorous controls: includes comparisons against random attention head interventions, gradient-based attribution, and random visual patch ablations, confirming the specificity of the localized heads and patches.
Validated across two distinct modern VLM architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b) with consistent findings.
Clarity in writing and presentation, with well-structured figures and transparent discussion of limitations and intervention side effects (e.g., caption degradation and KL divergence analysis).
weaknesses: The evaluation setup is restricted to single-token cloze-style completions at the prompt's final position, which simplifies natural generation dynamics and leaves multi-token or free-form reasoning unexplored.

The dataset size is relatively modest (~430 evaluated samples) and derives solely from WHOOPS!, focusing on visually absurd/counterfactual scenes rather than broader, real-world perceptual-knowledge conflict distributions.

The intervention framework relies on heuristically selected hyperparameters (e.g., fixing the intervention to the top 20 heads and bounding scaling factor λ ∈ [-3, 3]), which, while empirically justified, may limit generalizability across different prompt templates or tasks.

Reliance on the standard Logit Lens at intermediate layers can introduce projection artifacts and representational distortions, as noted in the limitations, which could be strengthened by comparisons with tuned lenses or activation patching.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: understanding the internal mechanistic dynamics of how vision-language models resolve conflicts between visual inputs and parametric commonsense knowledge.

Methodology is sound and thorough: the paper combines logit lens analysis, targeted causal interventions, and patch ablations, accompanied by thoughtful control experiments (e.g., intervening on random heads, intervening on MLPs).

Strong validation of head specificity: the authors demonstrate on the POPE benchmark that the identified counterfactual heads are specifically recruited under multimodal conflict rather than acting as generic visual processing heads.

Demonstrated transferability across datasets: replicating findings on the Visual CounterFact dataset shows high overlap in the identified heads, supporting the generalizability of the mechanistic circuit.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly organized, and transparent about limitations.
weaknesses: The analysis is strictly limited to next-token prediction / single-token completions, leaving open how these conflict-resolution mechanisms behave in multi-token autoregressive generation and free-form visual question answering.
The quantitative attribution evaluation against ground-truth segmentation masks (Section 5.4 and Appendix I) is evaluated on a relatively small sample of only 20 images.

Architectural coverage is restricted to late-fusion vision-language models (LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3); investigating whether early-fusion architectures or cross-attention architectures exhibit identical functional separation between MLPs and attention heads remains unexplored.

strengths: Compelling mechanistic framing: The paper provides a clear and principled investigation into the tension between parametric commonsense knowledge and conflicting visual context in VLMs, filling an important gap between text-only knowledge conflict literature and multimodal interpretability.

Methodological rigor and well-designed controls: The causal intervention pipeline is thoroughly validated with appropriate controls, including random attention head interventions (Fig. 11), validation against generic visual capability via the POPE benchmark (Table 3), and testing on an external dataset (Visual CounterFact).

Detailed attribution analysis: The comparison between attention patterns from identified conflict-mediating heads and standard gradient-based attribution is substantiated through both pixel ablation experiments (Fig. 5) and quantitative mask overlap evaluation using SAM-3 segmentations with statistical significance tests (Table 4).

High clarity and execution: The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and features high-quality figures that effectively convey the core findings across both tested architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B).
weaknesses: Restriction to single-token next-token prediction: The evaluation focuses on the last-token position completing a cloze-style prompt. While standard in mechanistic interpretability, this simplifies the multimodal interaction compared to multi-token free-form generation where knowledge conflict dynamics may evolve across autoregressive steps.

Dataset scale and diversity: WHOOPS-AHA! is derived from 500 source images from WHOOPS! resulting in 432–436 validated samples. While sufficient for statistical analysis in circuit discovery, the benchmark size is relatively modest.

Architectural coverage: Both examined models (LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3) belong to late-fusion autoregressive decoder architectures. Examining early-fusion or cross-attention based multimodal architectures would provide broader insight into the universality of the identified attention/MLP dissociation.

Formalization of intervention normalization: In Section 4.2 (Equations 1 and 2), the multiplicative factor is applied directly to attention weights after softmax. The manuscript would benefit from clarifying whether post-intervention attention weights are re-normalized across the row or propagated unnormalized.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question in multimodal NLP: how vision-language models mechanistically resolve conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and contradictory visual context.

Methodologically sound and thorough: combines observational probing (logit lens across layers, MLPs, and attention heads) with causal interventions (bidirectional attention weight steering) and patch-level ablations.

Comprehensive control experiments: includes random-head intervention controls, evaluation on POPE to demonstrate that counterfactual heads are conflict-specific rather than generic vision-processing heads, and fluency/KL-divergence checks on generation quality under varying intervention strengths.

Demonstrates cross-model and cross-dataset generalizability across two architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B) and shows substantial head overlap when transferring the analysis to the Visual CounterFact benchmark.

Provides an interesting connection between mechanistic interpretability and visual attribution, showing that attention patterns from counterfactual heads localize anomalous image regions more precisely than standard gradient-based attribution.
weaknesses: The scope of the benchmark is somewhat small: WHOOPS-AHA! is derived from 500 WHOOPS! images (yielding ~435 usable instances after filtering), and the quantitative segmentation evaluation in Section 5.4 / Appendix I is performed on only 20 sampled images.

The analysis is constrained to constrained single-token prompt continuations at the final token position; while this enables clean causal tracing, it leaves open how these mechanisms operate during multi-token, free-form reasoning or conversational VQA.

Evaluated architectures are restricted to late-fusion vision-language models, leaving it unclear how these conflict-resolution mechanisms behave in unified native multimodal or early/mid-fusion architectures.
